source_evidence.observation: The underlying system is homogeneous, first-order, linear, and constant-coefficient in one spatial dimension. The unknown q maps R × R to R^m, and A is a constant real m × m matrix. Subscripts denote partial derivatives.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 25; printed page 3; opening paragraph
source_evidence.anchor: hyperbolic if the matrix A has real eigenvalues and a corresponding set of m linearly independent eigenvectors
source_evidence.observation: Hyperbolicity requires a complete set of real characteristic speeds and linearly independent eigenvectors. Every vector in R^m has a unique expansion in these eigenvectors; the corresponding eigenvalues give wave propagation speeds.

contract_plain_english: For the one-dimensional homogeneous system q_t + A q_x = 0 with constant real A, hyperbolicity means that A has real eigenvalues and a complete set of independent eigenvectors (printed pp. 1 and 3). Give the system constant left and right initial states separated at x = 0, as in equation (1.11), leaving the value at the interface unspecified (printed p. 5). The source asserts that this linear hyperbolic Riemann problem can be solved using the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of A, referring to Chapter 3 for the construction (printed pp. 5–6). The surrounding description presents Riemann solutions as typically depending only on x/t and comprising finitely many waves with constant propagation speeds (printed p. 5); the earlier discussion identifies those speeds with eigenvalues and explains unique eigenvector decomposition (printed p. 3). These pages do not supply an explicit solution formula, a precise solution class, or a pointwise convention at wave discontinuities.
